own_scenes.place: Suburbios de Estados Unidos (Míchigan, Texas, Florida, Los Ángeles)
own_scenes.desc: En 1966 no tenían nombre (Billboard los llamaba «rockers»); hoy se les llama grupos de garaje. La respuesta creativa americana a la invasión británica: chicos blancos de suburbio que ensayaban en el garaje familiar y tocaban en gimnasios, iglesias y fiestas, con cortes de pelo de Brian Jones, actitud de Jagger, fuzz, rave-ups a lo Yardbirds, Them y Stones y, casi siempre, un órgano Farfisa o Vox con un regusto siniestro de película de terror de autocine. Recuperaban la línea del rock americano de 1963-1964 (Kingsmen, Trashmen) que los Beatles cortaron en seco: «Hanky Panky» de Tommy James, grabado en 1963, fue número 1 en julio de 1966. Ese septiembre las listas se llenaron de discos duros: «96 Tears» de ? and the Mysterians (mexicanoamericanos de Flint, con un órgano hipnótico de otro disco), «Dirty Water» de los Standells, «You’re Gonna Miss Me» de los 13th Floor Elevators y «Psychotic Reaction» de Count Five, calco del «I’m a Man» de los Yardbirds. Quejas dirigidas a las mujeres, pero también una nueva confianza; quejas pequeñas que empezaban a encontrar un objetivo, como en «One of These Days» de los Roosters.

refs.q: On first hearing, ? and the Mysterians’ ‘96 Tears’ is all wrong
refs.para: On first hearing, ? and the Mysterians’ ‘96 Tears’ is all wrong: the tempo is slow and shaky, the singer is Jaggeresque in a particularly flagrant way, and the predominant organ backing, as Penny Valentine wrote at the time, sounds as if it comes ‘from another record’. But it quickly reveals its charms, as the organ transcends relentlessness to become hypnotic, its clusters of repeated notes echoing the lyrical mantra of obsession and revenge: ‘You’re gonna cry, cry, cry, cry.’
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: Garage bands, they’re called today, but there was no single name for this style in 1966.
refs.para: Garage bands, they’re called today, but there was no single name for this style in 1966. Billboard called most of them ‘rockers’ in the capsule reviews, and that’s what they were: the original wildness, attack and teenage intensity of rock ’n’ roll updated ten years on. It’s no accident that Tommy James and the Shondells’ ‘Hanky Panky’ was such a big hit that summer: recorded in 1963, it captured the exact moment when white American music was flourishing, just before the Beatles revolutionised the country’s teen taste.
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: There was one element that distinguished the American rockers from their UK counterparts
refs.para: There was one element that distinguished the American rockers from their UK counterparts: the almost ubiquitous use of the electric organ – usually a Farfisa or a Vox Continental – which usually gave a sinuous, if not sinister, undertow to proceedings. In the mid-1960s, the drive-in was a major teen venue in the US, and a constant diet of horror movies satisfied both the needs for sexual experimentation and the perennial teen penchant for living at the extremes.
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: One record in particular caught that moment of compression.
refs.para: One record in particular caught that moment of compression. Released in mid-1966, the Roosters’ ‘One of These Days’ was perfectly poised between glistening Byrds twelve-string jangle and surf kinetics, between high Hollies harmonies and punk-mystical lead vocals, between teen yearning and universal protest: ‘One of these days when I’m of age / And nobody can tell me what to do.’
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

podcast.title: Origins and Original Era (1964-1968)
podcast.body: The roots of Garage Rock trace back to the early 1960s, sparked by inspiration from The Beatles and the British Invasion. Initially, it was simply called "Rock," not "Garage Rock." Its golden age was between 1964 (especially after The Beatles' Ed Sullivan appearance) and around 1968, when rock became more polished. An estimated 184,000 Garage bands formed in the US during those four years alone. "The roots of Garage Rock began in the early 1960s, when bands inspired by the Beatles and the rest of the British invasion started springing up like mushrooms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Decline of Original Era (c. 1968)
podcast.body: The original Garage Rock era concluded around 1968, largely influenced by technological advancements in recording studios that led to more sophisticated recordings. Rock bands themselves became more refined in their live performances, songwriting, and overall presentation. The rise of the album format also contributed, as Garage Rock had primarily found success through 7-inch singles and struggled to adapt to albums, which became the preferred format with the shift from AM to FM radio. "The original garage rock era ended around 1968, largely because of technology."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: "Farmer John" as a Standard
podcast.body: Dillon Di's "Farmer John" had not yet become a garage rock standard until The Searchers' version was released on their debut album, which is credited for largely popularizing it within the genre. "Farmer John by Dillon Dui, which hadn't yet become a garage rock standard, and indeed seems to have become so largely because of the searches version."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: 2000s Revival Movement
podcast.body: In the early 2000s, as mainstream rock became increasingly overproduced, a scene of bands emerged that deliberately returned to the rawer roots of rock. They revived the wild, low-fi sound of 1960s garage rock, emphasizing a more primitive and simple musical approach. "Recuperaron el sonido Loof-Fight, salvaje del garage rock de los 60s, rescataron la simplicidad del punk de los 70s, y revitalizaron los bajos gruesos y las límicas trotonas del Poppunk de los 80s."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué White Stripes desaparecieron en su mejor momento?

podcast.title: Antiquity and Cyclical Nature
podcast.body: Garage rock is nearly as old as rock music itself, having first emerged in the early 1960s. Since then, it has consistently ebbed and flowed through the decades, experiencing constant revivals. "It is almost as old as rock itself. And since it first emerged in the early 1960s, it has ebbed and flowed constantly through the decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 3: Emo

podcast.title: Biggest Revival (Late 1990s/Early 2000s)
podcast.body: The most significant Garage Rock revival since punk occurred at the end of the 1990s and into the early 2000s. This resurgence was spurred by a disillusionment with the state of alternative rock, the burnout of grunge, the polarizing nature of nu-metal, and the dominance of pop music. It began in New York, with bands like The Strokes and The White Stripes, and coincided with a post-9/11 shift in public taste and youth seeking music with "more teeth, more bite." "This is what happened with Garage Rock at the very end of the 1990s in the early 2000s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Cyclical Revival (Late 1960s, Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Garage rock from the late 1960s played a role in the lineage of the Indie Rock Revival of the early 2000s, serving as a foundational style that was "repeated" and combined with punk. Bands like The Hives were part of this later revival. "which itself was a repeat of the garage rock of the late 60s, made it with a punk in the mid 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Definition
podcast.body: Garage Rock is defined as basic, raw, loose, ragged rock and roll, primarily featuring guitar, bass, drums, vocals, and often a thin-sounding Farfisa organ. It is typically unsophisticated, primal, and primitive, built around power or bar chords, and can sometimes be aggressive, played in informal settings like basements, rec rooms, or garages. "It's the basic, raw, loose, ragged rock and roll you and your buddies play for no reason other than it feels good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Early Canadian Example
podcast.body: Garage rock was a genre that saw a "very solid" Canadian example in 1965 with a single from a Winnipeg band that would later become The Guess Who. Despite its quality, it was initially dismissed by radio stations simply because it was Canadian, highlighting the historical bias against homegrown music. "In 1965, a band from Winnipeg released a very solid garage rock single."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Fanzine Coverage (1960s)
podcast.body: The fanzine "Punk," which appeared at the end of 1975, covered "raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s" like Question Mark and the Mysterians, recognizing their influence on the emerging punk scene. "It also covered Iggy Pop and the Stooges, The New York Dolls, and even some of their raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s like Question Mark and Mysterians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3

podcast.title: First Revival: Punk Rock (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: The punk rock explosion of the mid-1970s is recognized as the first revival of Garage Rock. This new incarnation was essentially the same fundamental sound, but typically louder, sometimes angrier, occasionally political, and often much faster, while maintaining its core DNA. Bands like the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and The Damned are considered Garage Rock at their core due to their back-to-basics approach. "So the punk rock explosion of the middle 70s was the first ever revival of garage rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Influence of Revivals
podcast.body: Each time garage rock has experienced a revival and re-emerged into prominence, it has exerted a significant influence on the prevailing music of that era. "And each time it's come up for air, it's had a major influence on the music of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 3: Emo

podcast.title: Influence on Shoegaze
podcast.body: Garage rock exerted strong influences on the shoegaze sound, contributing significantly to its noisy and guitar-driven characteristics. "tenía como esas influencias muy fortes del garaje que podía ser de sonidjuz o de esa parte del roca americano."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Minor Revival: Garage Punk (Late 1980s/Early 1990s)
podcast.body: After the punk explosion and its subsequent diversification in the 1980s, a minor revival emerged in the late 1980s and early 1990s, labeled "Garage Punk." These bands, such as The Headcoats, The Mighty Caesars, and The Mummies, drew more heavily from The Stooges than The Kingsmen, resulting in a louder and faster sound compared to the original Garage Rock acts. "After the punk explosion and its segmentation and stratification into many different forms throughout the 1980s, there was a minor revival in the late 80s and early 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Mixed with Pop Punk in 2010s
podcast.body: Garage Rock elements were sometimes added to Pop Punk styles by "culty bands" in the 2010s. This mix created a harder edge for these bands, such as Wavves, Bass Drum of Death, Ty Segall, and PUP, contributing to the brief surge of Pop Punk during the decade. "And if you were inclined to look, you would have also found some interesting culty bands who plumbed Pop Punk styles and occasionally took things a little harder and then also maybe add a little garage rock to the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Pacific Northwest Scene (Late 50s/Early 60s)
podcast.body: Much of the music classified as Garage Rock or Frat Rock originated from the vibrant and innovative Pacific Northwest music scene of the late 1950s and early 1960s, which saw mostly white musicians performing their own electric guitar versions of music by black artists. "much of the music that gets labeled Gavage Rock or Frat Rock comes from that area."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 106:"Louie Louie" by the Kingsmen

podcast.title: Persistent Underground Presence
podcast.body: Garage Rock is characterized as an enduring underground phenomenon that consistently resurfaces into the mainstream at unexpected times and in unforeseen ways. Its long history suggests it is a lasting genre, always "bubbling up" and awaiting its next revival. "Garage Rock seems to be an underground thing that is always there. Something that's always bubbling up into the mainstream in unexpected ways at unexpected times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Phenomenological Movement
podcast.body: Garage Rock was not a formal genre with a unified aesthetic but rather a phenomenological movement characterized by a clear attitude. It involved young people from working-class neighborhoods, often without formal musical training, who created profoundly energetic, direct, and raw songs. Many were teenagers imitating bands like The Rolling Stones or The Kinks, but their lack of training and access to professional studios or equipment resulted in a distinct lo-fi, distortion-laden sound. "No era un genero formal, ni tenía una estética unificada, pero sí que compartía una actitud clara."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Pioneered by Joey D and the Starlighters
podcast.body: The stripped-down version of R&B performed by Joey D and the Starlighters, characterized by the organ as its dominant instrument, was a precursor to what would later become known as Garage Rock. "The kind of thing that would later get known as Garage Rock or Frat Rock."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 91: "The Twist" by Chubby Checker

podcast.title: Ramones' Sound Influence
podcast.body: The core of The Ramones' music was described as "bubblegum pop mixed with 60s garage rock played at a million miles an hour," defining their distinct, fast-paced style. "at its core, this music was bubblegum pop mixed with 60s garage rock played at a million miles an hour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3

podcast.title: Rebellion Against Melodic Innocence
podcast.body: In the Garage Rock movement, the melodic innocence associated with The Beatles was explicitly replaced by an expression of rage, alienation, and noise. This shift reflected a more visceral and confrontational approach to music, embodying a youthful rebellion against the polished sounds of the mainstream. "La inocencia melodica de los Beatles fue reemplazada por la rabia, la alinación y el ruido."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Regional Diversity
podcast.body: Garage Rock lacked a single, unified sound, instead exhibiting strong regional variations across different areas. For instance, Surf Rock developed distinctly on the American West Coast. "There was no one sound for Garage Rock bands. Everything was very regional."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Revival in Early 2000s
podcast.body: Around the time The Strokes' debut album "Is This It" was gaining traction, there was significant talk about a garage rock revival. This movement, often associated with a "new look at an old sound," was seen as a key component of the broader Indy Rock Revival. "People were talking about a garage rock revival and the return of Indy Rock and a new look at an old sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Strokes

podcast.title: Simple Rebellious Vibe
podcast.body: Garage rock typically features two or three chords played on guitar, bass, and drums, characterized by a loose, rebellious vibe that prioritizes feeling good over complexity. "Garage rock, two or three chords played on guitar, bass and drums with a loose rebellious vibe. Nothing too complicated. It's just gotta feel good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Surf Music

podcast.title: Sonic Compatibility with Cassette
podcast.body: The inherent "reduced sound" quality of cassette tapes has made it a characteristic and attractive medium for genres like garage rock. This specific sound, though not objectively pure, is appreciated by passionate fans who find it suitable for their music. "el sonido del caset es como un sonido que se ha hecho muy característico en ciertos estilos de música como puede ser el rock de garage."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Coleccionar Cassettes. Cosas que hay que saber.
